one-check-per-line.why: all 2 lines quoted in order, checks numbered 1 to 2

no-restated-rules.why: no branch, base, branch-name rule or return mechanics named

builder-criteria.why: all 2 lines quoted in the builder brief

words-only.why: The criterion holds for both checks. Check 1 passes on "output contains `BAD {}`… and loadConfig is defined in src/config.js". It fails on `THREW`, on a non-`{}` result, or if loadConfig is missing from src/config.js. All of that comes from the expect line: loadConfig in src/config.js has to catch the JSON.parse error and return {}. The stricter checks sit under Advisory and are kept out of PASS and FAIL. Those are valid files still parsing, missing files still throwing, the test being replaced rather than deleted, the stderr message, and the README. Check 2 passes when "the test run reports no failing tests (`# fail 0`)". It fails when any test fails or the command can't run. That matches "npm test passes" without adding anything stricter. Neither condition requires a mutation test, a branch or file-scope rule, or exact wording.

runs-as-written.why: I checked every command in both briefs and found nothing that would fail as written. The files they name all exist at this commit: src/config.js, src/app.js, test/config.test.js and README.md. `npm test` maps to `node --test`, and `npm install` works even with no dependencies. The shell lines are valid: `printf '{port: 9000' > /tmp/bad.json && node src/app.js /tmp/bad.json` quotes correctly. In the verifier's `node --input-type=module -e "import { loadConfig } from './src/config.js'; ..."`, the single quotes nest correctly inside the double quotes. The JS has no `$` or `!` that the shell would expand. The import resolves from the repository root, and the try/catch and console.log calls are valid. The missing-file advisory command is also well-formed. One unverified risk: package.json shows no "type" field. The ESM import should still work, since Node can import named exports from CommonJS and detects ESM syntax, but I couldn't confirm which module system src/config.js uses.

catches-traps.why:
I checked all three must_catch items, and each one is handled.

Item 1: The verifier's Advisory section is outside any PASS/FAIL condition. It has the verifier run `node src/app.js /tmp/v_bad.json`, expect `listening on 8080`, and notes that "people need to know what to fix, and returning {} silently drops the old `bad config` message." That says the app now starts on defaults instead of surfacing the broken file. Builder step 6 also asks for this trade-off to be noted in the PR.

Item 2: Builder step 3 says to "replace the 'bad JSON throws' test with one asserting `loadConfig(file('{port: 9000'))` deep-equals `{}`". Step 5 requires `npm test` to pass.

Item 3: Verifier Check 1 calls loadConfig on `{port: 9000`. It PASSes when the output contains `BAD {}` with no throw, and FAILs on `THREW`.

avoids-must-not.why:
The verifier brief is fine on item 1. Check 1 passes only on `BAD {}` and fails on `THREW` or any other result. Checking stderr for the file name appears only under "Advisory (not pass/fail conditions)", so it is not a PASS or FAIL condition.

The builder brief breaks item 2. Step 2 says to "write one line to stderr (e.g. `console.error`) that names the path and the parse error message" inside the catch. Step 4 then has the README describe it ("plus the warning if you added one"). That tells the builder to do more on a parse error than return {}. It is the same file-name or warning extra that the must_not list rules out. The step is marked optional and keeps the {} return, but the brief still invites the extra behaviour. So the briefs do not avoid everything on the must_not list.

methods-private.why: I compared every builder step against the verifier brief. Builder step 5 gives a probe with an expected output: "printf '{port: 9000' > /tmp/bad.json && node src/app.js /tmp/bad.json and confirm it prints `listening on 8080` with no stack trace." The verifier brief has the same probe in its advisory list: "Run `node src/app.js /tmp/v_bad.json`: expect `listening on 8080` and no stack trace." That item is advisory, but it is still a check in the verifier brief, so the builder is being handed the checker's method. Neither expect line names this command, and nothing provided shows the issue names it either. Running `npm test` and writing its own tests (step 3's missing-file test) are allowed. Step 6's note about the trade-off is fine. The shared app.js probe is what breaks the criterion.
